title: Charging by the Second: Globacom's Late Entry Into Nigeria, 2003
dek: Two years after losing his first mobile licence, Mike Adenuga's Globacom launched in Nigeria billing calls by the second instead of by the minute.

story.event: Launching Glo Mobile in August 2003 with per-second billing, after losing a GSM licence in 2001
story.summary: In 2001 Mike Adenuga's Communications Investments lost one of Nigeria's four GSM licences after the regulator said the $285 million fee was not paid in time. In August 2002 his Globacom won the second national operator licence, and on 29 August 2003 it launched Glo Mobile with per-second billing, when rivals charged about N50 per minute or part of one; competitors followed. Glo reached 600,000 subscribers in six months; two decades later its share had fallen to about 13 per cent and it appointed outside management in 2024.
paragraphs: In 2001 Mike Adenuga, a Nigerian businessman with interests in oil and banking, lost his first mobile licence before he had built anything. His company, Communications Investments, had been one of four winners of Nigeria's auction of GSM licences, each priced at $285 million and payable within 14 days. The regulator said the money had not been deposited in time and took the licence away. The company contested the finding, and ThisDay later reported that its $20 million deposit was lost too. MTN and Econet launched that year.

The next chance was a different licence. In August 2002 Adenuga's Globacom won the right to become Nigeria's second national operator, covering mobile, fixed lines and an international gateway. By then Nigerians knew the incumbents' prices well: a pay-as-you-go caller paid N50 whether a call lasted one second or sixty, on networks where calls often dropped. According to ThisDay, the established operators had said billing by the second was technically impossible in Nigeria.

Glo's mobile network was delayed for months. When it went live on 29 August 2003, two years behind its rivals, it charged by the second, kept per-minute plans for those who preferred them and undercut competitors on the price of a line. Thousands signed up; in Abuja, many who missed out bought lines in Lagos a month later. In early 2004 Glo's executives told US diplomats that per-second billing had played a key role, and that the money lay in how long customers stayed on air, not in what they paid to join. Rivals soon moved to per-second billing too.

By the end of February 2004 Glo had 600,000 subscribers in 49 cities, and executives put spending on its networks at about $1.2 billion. The diplomats also recorded doubts: the rollout had cost more than planned, and observers said financing had been hard to secure. Two decades on, the early lead had faded. In 2024, after the regulator tightened the rules for counting active lines, Glo removed about 40 million inactive subscribers, leaving 19.1 million and about 13 per cent of the market. That October, under pressure from the regulator, it named a new chief executive and board.

quote.text: Wealth is in applications of mind to nature, and the art of getting rich consists not in industry, much less in saving, but in a better order, in timeliness, in being at the right spot.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Emerson credits wealth to a better order, to timeliness and to being in the right spot. Adenuga's story bends the line both ways: a missed deadline cost him one licence, and arriving two years late let him offer what the first operators had called impossible. Being on time and being in time were different things.

reflection: Glo did not win its early customers by being first. It arrived after two established rivals and built its offer around a complaint every caller already had: paying for a full minute that a dropped call never delivered. Being late gave it a long, clear look at that complaint.

If you feel behind, at work or anywhere else, it may help to notice what those ahead of you have taught people to put up with. Lateness has real costs, and Adenuga paid one in 2001. But arriving second can also mean arriving knowing exactly what is wrong.
invitation: Write down one small thing the people you serve have quietly learned to put up with. This week, ask one of them whether it bothers them as much as you think it does.

sources.title: Nigeria: Globacom: Six Months On (US Consulate Lagos cable 04LAGOS676, 26 March 2004)
sources.publisher: WikiLeaks cable as published by Scoop
sources.supports: Second national operator licences (mobile, fixed and international gateway) won in August 2002; lengthy delays rolling out the mobile network; the 29 August launch attracting thousands, with many who missed lines in Abuja buying them in Lagos a month later; 600,000 subscribers in six months and 49 major cities; executives' estimate of about $1.2 billion spent; Globacom the first Nigerian GSM operator to offer per-second billing, with a choice of per-second or per-minute plans and executives saying it played a key role; cheaper lines than MTN; executives' view that money is made from time on air rather than subscription; spending above plan, observers' doubts about financing.

sources.title: Nigerian operators race for first-place launch: One licensee loses spectrum
sources.supports: Four GSM licence winners including Communications Investments Nigeria; each to pay the $285 million fee within 14 days; Communications Investments failed to make the deposit and forfeited its licence; the company contested the commission's findings; its spectrum to go to a future second national operator.

sources.title: The stunning decline of Globacom
sources.publisher: TechCabal (Frank Eleanya and Olumuyiwa Olowogboyega, 12 November 2024)
sources.supports: Launch in August 2003, two years behind MTN, Econet and Mtel; per-second billing against the N50-per-minute norm, forcing rivals to follow; the 2024 recount under the regulator's 90-day inactivity rule removing about 40 million subscribers, leaving 19.1 million and a 13 per cent share; a new CEO and board in October 2024 after pressure from the NCC; Adenuga widely believed to be the company's sole financier.

sources.title: X-raying Glo's Impact in Telecoms Sector at 19
sources.supports: Communications Investments as one of four auction winners; the $20 million deposit paid and lost when the licence was revoked; the second national operator licence won in August 2002 through Globacom; launch with per-second billing, which older operators had said was not possible; mass rollout and more than one million subscribers within nine months.

sources.title: The Man Who Never Takes No for an Answer
sources.supports: Pay-as-you-go callers paying at least N50 per call from 2001 whether it lasted one second or a minute; poor connections; the networks saying per-second billing was technologically impossible; Glo's per-second billing and other networks then adopting it; Adenuga's oil company and banks; the 2001 CIL licence revoked and $20 million deposit lost over the payment deadline; the 2002 second national carrier licence.

sources.title: Eight years of Glo, 8 giant strides for Nigeria
sources.supports: N50-per-minute tariffs and dropped calls before Glo; CIL losing its bid to become an operator; Globacom awarded the second national operator licence in 2002 covering GSM, national carrier and international gateway; per-second charging from launch, with competitors following.

cross_checks.claim: In 2001 Adenuga's Communications Investments lost its GSM licence over the unpaid licence fee.
Globacom won the second national operator licence in August 2002.
Glo Mobile launched on 29 August 2003 as the first Nigerian GSM operator to bill per second.
Incumbents charged about N50 per minute or part of one, and rivals followed Glo to per-second billing.

research_notes: Adenuga rarely speaks publicly, and no interview with him was used; the reasoning behind per-second billing is attributed to Glo executives as reported in the March 2004 US consulate cable, and paraphrased because the cable itself paraphrases them. Several Nigerian sources (ThisDay 2022 and 2023, Vanguard 2011) are anniversary or tribute pieces and are used only for widely reported facts, not for praise or for claims about political motives. Licence fee and date: RCR Wireless (July 2001) gives $285 million payable within 14 days and says Communications Investments failed to deposit it and contested the finding; ThisDay (2023) gives a $265 million balance after a $20 million deposit and says the deadline was missed 'by a few hours'; ThisDay (2022) dates a conditional licence to 1999. The story uses RCR's figures and attributes the lost deposit to ThisDay. Line prices differ (the cable gives N6,000 for a Glo prepaid line against MTN's N6,480; ThisDay 2022 gives a cut from N30,000 to N6,999), so the story says only that Glo undercut rivals on the price of a line. Subscriber growth: 600,000 in six months and 49 cities per the cable (executives' figures), more than one million within nine months per ThisDay 2022; the story uses the cable. The $1.2 billion is executives' estimate as reported in the cable. Exact dates on which Econet and MTN adopted per-second billing (late 2003 in one secondary source that no longer loads) are not used; the story says rivals soon followed. The cable's insiders also criticised Adenuga's management style; that is not used, as it is anonymous and outside the episode. The 2024 figures rest on TechCabal alone and are not treated as pivotal; Mobility Nigeria's later figure (23.47 million subscribers and 12.4 per cent share in May 2026) is not used. Funding is set to 'unknown': the company is privately held and TechCabal says Adenuga is widely believed to be its sole financier, but how the $1.2 billion rollout was financed is not documented in the sources.
